question:
Let $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{a,b\}$. A function $f:A\times B\to B\times A$ is defined by $f(x,y)=(y,x)$. Thus, the function reverses the order of the two components of every ordered pair. The domain contains the six pairs $(1,a),(1,b),(2,a),(2,b),(3,a),(3,b)$, while the codomain contains the corresponding reversed pairs. Students investigate whether two different ordered pairs can acquire the same image and whether every possible ordered pair in $B\times A$ is obtained through this rule.

(a) Find $f(2,a)$ and $f(3,b)$.

(b) If $f(x_1,y_1)=f(x_2,y_2)$, determine the relation between $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$.

(c) Given an arbitrary $(y,x)\in B\times A$, find a pre-image under $f$.

(d) Hence determine whether $f$ is one-one and onto.
explanation:
(a)
By the rule $f(x,y)=(y,x)$, we obtain $f(2,a)=(a,2)$ and $f(3,b)=(b,3)$.

(b)
Suppose $f(x_1,y_1)=f(x_2,y_2)$. Then $(y_1,x_1)=(y_2,x_2)$. Equality of ordered pairs gives $y_1=y_2$ and $x_1=x_2$. Hence $(x_1,y_1)=(x_2,y_2)$. Therefore, $f$ is one-one.

(c)
Let $(y,x)$ be an arbitrary element of $B\times A$. Since $x\in A$ and $y\in B$, the ordered pair $(x,y)$ belongs to $A\times B$. Also, $f(x,y)=(y,x)$. Thus, $(x,y)$ is a pre-image of $(y,x)$.

(d)
Part (b) proves that $f$ is one-one. Part (c) proves that every element of $B\times A$ has a pre-image in $A\times B$, so $f$ is onto. Therefore, $f$ is both one-one and onto.

options.A: $f(2,a)=(2,a)$ and $f(3,b)=(3,b)$; equal images do not imply equal inputs, and $f$ is neither one-one nor onto.
options.B: $f(2,a)=(a,2)$ and $f(3,b)=(b,3)$; equal images imply equal inputs, but some elements of $B\times A$ have no pre-image, so $f$ is one-one but not onto.
options.C: $f(2,a)=(a,2)$ and $f(3,b)=(b,3)$; equal images imply $(x_1,y_1)=(x_2,y_2)$, and the pre-image of $(y,x)$ is $(x,y)$. Hence, $f$ is both one-one and onto.
options.D: $f(2,a)=(a,3)$ and $f(3,b)=(b,2)$; every codomain element has a pre-image, but distinct inputs may have the same image, so $f$ is onto but not one-one.
